title: Rapid prototyping and fabrication method for 3-D food objects

report.headline: Dead patent with a future: a lapsed 2001 patent on 3D-printing food layer by layer, in a field that still looks active, scoring 78/100 with high confidence.
report.what_it_is: This patent covers a method for printing a food object from a computer design. A nozzle squeezes out a paste, like cake batter or icing, layer by layer onto a platform, and the paste firms up fast enough to hold its shape before an optional baking step.

why_it_died.text: The owner paid the first two maintenance fees, then stopped paying the third one. The patent lapsed in 2013, about 7 years before it would have expired anyway. The record does not say why they stopped. Not paying a fee is usually a business decision, not proof the idea was bad. But it also does not prove the idea was good, which is why 'Died for money, not merit' scored only 5.2 out of 15. No reinstatement appears on record.

case_for.point: The field appears to still be alive. Later filings kept building on this patent long after it lapsed, including some from 2019 onward. That is why 'Field still alive' scored a full 30/30 and 'Recent momentum' scored 15.2/20.
Real food companies seem interested. Frito-Lay, Redefine Meat (alternative meat) and a German food-tech institute have filed on top of this patent since 2019.
Patent examiners treated it as important prior work. They cited it against 80 later applications, which suggests it describes a foundational technique.

Someone already sells a product in this space. Natural Machines markets the Foodini printer to restaurants, hotels, texture-modified diets for people who have trouble swallowing, and education. That may show paying customers exist in specific niches.

case_against.point: An existing product means you would likely face a competitor on day one. You would need a clear niche or a better approach than the Foodini.
Interest is not the same as a market. The evidence shows filings and one product, but nothing on market size or revenue.

The patent was filed in only one country, so it says little about how the idea was treated elsewhere. Its claims are also long (shortest is 172 words), so they were fairly narrow. That fits the middling 7.8/15 breadth score.
Several newer, still-active-looking filings build on this idea. The valuable improvements may sit in those newer patents, not in this old one.

blockers.point: Later patents by other owners may still be in force. Examiners cited 71 of them against this one. Any of them could cover parts of a modern food printer or process.

Specific food pastes, ingredient recipes or process settings may be patented separately, even if the basic printing method is not. Recent filers like Frito-Lay and Redefine Meat may hold some of these.
The patent explains the idea, not how to make it work reliably. Expect to work out paste recipes, temperatures and nozzle settings yourself.
No reinstatement is on record, which looks good. Still, the status should be confirmed against current official records. These facts come from an archived web snapshot from October 2024.

assumption_to_test.assumption: A specific niche, such as care homes serving texture-modified meals or bakeries making custom cake decorations, will pay for a food-printing product or service instead of buying an existing printer like the Foodini or decorating by hand.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The technical idea appears proven and the field active. What is not shown is whether any niche will pay enough, and why they would choose you over an existing product. Without that, nothing else matters.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: Pick one niche. Do 15 to 20 short interviews with buyers, such as care home kitchen managers or bakery owners. Ask how they handle the task today, what it costs, and whether they looked at the Foodini and why they did or did not buy. Run a $200 landing page with a price and a 'request a pilot' button, aimed at that niche. Success means at least 3 buyers who state a concrete budget or agree to a paid pilot.

attorney_questions: Can you confirm from current official records that US6280785B1 and the related US6280784B1 lapsed and were never reinstated, and that no other family members exist?

Which of the 71 later patents cited against this one, and the recent filings by Frito-Lay, Redefine Meat and others, appear to still be in force and may be worth reviewing for our planned product, materials and process?
If we develop our own food paste recipes and process settings, what should we do to document them, and is any of it worth protecting with our own filings or as trade secrets?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: Sustained technical interest after lapse: the patent remains a frequently cited foundation for food 3D printing, with most citations coming from unrelated owners after it lapsed.

Recent but modest momentum: a small number of new filings since 2019 build on it, including from a large snack company and an alternative-protein firm, suggesting continued exploration in snacks and plant-based meat.

A commercial product exists in the space: Natural Machines sells the Foodini 3D food printer into hospitality, texture-modified diets, education and seafood R&D, which indicates some market activity, though not its scale.

The original owner stopped paying maintenance fees about 7 years before the term would have ended, which may mean it saw limited commercial value at the time. The patent was also filed in only one jurisdiction.

read.who_is_active: Recent filers citing this patent include Frito-Lay North America, Redefine Meat, DIL Deutsches Institut für Lebensmitteltechnik, Triex LLC and an individual inventor (刘文海), and Natural Machines markets the Foodini food printer.
read.market_read: Food 3D printing remains technically alive, with steady citation activity and niche commercial uses such as personalized and texture-modified food, alternative proteins and hospitality decoration. The evidence shows interest and at least one product on the market, but it does not establish market size or revenue, so a founder should validate demand in a specific niche before committing.
